newsitem.title: USA: Three more added to jury pool in Broin smoke case.
newsitem.headline: Three more added to jury pool in Broin smoke case.

text.p: Three more prospective jurors were added Tuesday to a growing pool from which a jury will be picked to hear a landmark $5 billion lawsuit brought by flight attendants against the tobacco industry.

The new members brought to 40 the number of prospects approved during initial questioning for a jury to heard the lawsuit known as Broin vs. Philip Morris et al. The suit seeks damages from nine tobacco companies and industry groups on behalf of some 60,000 flight attendants who say they were made ill by secondhand smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.
With each side allowed to exclude 27 potential jurors, a pool of 60 is needed to choose a six-member panel, plus additional candidates to serve as alternates.
Dade County Judge Robert Kaye has yet to decide on the number of alternates to be selected.

The questioning of one jury candidate provoked a squabble among lawyers and a stern lecture from Kaye. The woman, a realtor with four children, said she would advise her kids not to smoke and offered that she was "glad that they have put a caution on (cigarette) packages."

One statement on her juror questionnaire appeared to disturb tobacco company lawyers. "Surely if there were not tobacco companies that flourish on the sale of tobacco, there would be no smokers," she wrote.

Industry lawyers asked her repeatedly if, given that statement, she could be a fair juror. "All I can say is that I would try," she said. Plaintiffs' attorney Stanley Rosenblatt objected to the questioning, prompting an angry exchange and a caution from Kaye, who said he would not have the lawyers bickering in front of jurors.
Tobacco lawyers asked that the woman be excused, but Kaye admitted her to the pool.

Another prospect found acceptable was a non-smoker who works as a truck driver for a soft drink company. He said he did not know if health warnings on cigarette packages were true. "As I sit here today I cannot answer that question honestly."
A non-smoker, the man said he opposed bans on smoking in public places, allowed people to smoke in his car and would not advise his children one way or another about smoking.
